1.goal: To open on a question she is already being asked often: what she wants to do in the future.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether she wrote the three questions for Nina.
Say what today is: a conversation with someone new about herself, her plans and a series or movie she watches, done once now and once again at the end of the lesson.
Ask the question on the screen and let her answer freely.
exact: What today is: “Today you meet someone new. You talk about you, what you want to do, and a series or a movie you like. We do it now, and again at the end of the lesson, and then we compare.”
After her answer: “Who asks you most? And what do you usually say?”
1.expected: A number or an idea of how often, and who asks. For example: “Lots of times. My parents ask me every week, and my teachers too.” or “Many times — everyone at school talks about it.”
1.support: If she does not answer, ask who asks her most often: family, school, or people she has just met.
1.challenge: Ask what she usually answers, and whether that answer is true.
1.monitoring: Whether the subject is something she wants to talk about. Her profile says she often talks about choosing a course and a career.
1.evidence: How she talks about the question itself. It helps you decide how much to push on screen 11.
1.transition: Move on when she knows the conversation happens twice: now, and at the end of the lesson.

2.goal: To set the situation and the person, so that the first try has a context: who Nina is, what she wants to know, and that the break is short.
run: Read Nina's card with her.
Ask the question on the screen: what can she tell and ask Nina first, and what can she say later?
Let her list the ideas in her own words. Do not discuss how to say them yet; that comes after the first try.
exact: After reading the card: “You have a short break with Nina. What can you tell and ask her first, and what can you say later?”
2.expected: Four or five ideas, in any order, for example: what she studies, and what that means in a Brazilian school; what she wants to do after school; why that, and not something else; a series or movie she likes, and what she thinks of it; something she wants to know about Nina. The reason for what she wants to do and the question back are the two ideas people often leave out.
2.support: If she lists only one or two ideas, ask what she would want to hear first if she were the one who had just arrived in another country.
2.challenge: Ask what Nina will want to ask next if she only hears what Gabriela studies.
2.monitoring: Whether she includes a reason and a question back without being prompted.
2.evidence: What she thinks can wait. It often shows what she will leave out on screen 3.
2.transition: Move on when she has said what comes first and what can wait.
2.tempo_na_tela: The short break is part of the scene: it tells her the conversation is short and informal. It is not a time limit on her speech, and no other screen shows a time.

3.goal: To see what she can already say in this conversation before any model or support.
3.interaction: T–S. You are Nina; she talks about herself.
run: Say you are Nina, and start with the first prompt below.
Listen, and let her say as much as she can. Leave corrections for screen 12, after the whole conversation.
If she stops and cannot continue, ask one of Nina's questions from the second prompt, and then listen again.
While she speaks, note roughly how many sentences she says, whether she gives a reason, whether she says what she thinks of a series or movie, and whether she asks you anything.
exact: Starting it: “Hi, I am Nina. The break is about to end. Tell me about you.”
If she stops, one question at a time: “So what do you want to do after school?” · “And what are you watching at the moment?”
3.expected: A short conversation with some information about her. A complete answer at this point could be: “I am Gabriela. I am in my last year of school. I want to study… because… I am watching… and I like it because… What about you?” She may give only two or three sentences and no reason; that is useful information for the rest of the lesson.
3.support: No language support on this screen, because it shows what she can already say. If she stops completely, ask one of Nina's questions from the prompt above.
3.challenge: If she speaks easily, ask one more question that she did not plan, for example: “Why that series?”
3.monitoring: Number of sentences, whether a reason appears, whether she gives an opinion about a series or movie, and what she does when she does not know what to say.
3.evidence: Her first try: the number of sentences, and whether there was a reason, an opinion and a question back. You compare it with screen 11.
3.transition: Move on when the conversation comes to a stop. Do not comment on it yet; say that you will come back to it.

4.goal: To read four questions Nina can ask, check which ones she can answer, and name the hard one.
4.interaction: T–S, reading the four out loud.
run: Read the questions on the screen with her: can she answer all of them, and which one is hard?
Read Nina's four questions out loud, one at a time. After each one, let her give a short answer out loud.
Ask which one was the hard one, and what made it hard.
If she cannot answer the fourth question now, that is fine: screen 7 gives her ways to answer it.
exact: After each question: “Can you answer this one? Try it.”
At the end: “Which one was the hard one? Why?”
4.expected: Short answers to the first three, for example: “I am in my last year.” · “I want to study… because…” · “I am watching… It is good, because…”. The hard one is usually the fourth, “What if it does not work out?”: it is hard because she may not have an answer yet, not because the words are difficult. Some students say the third is hard because they need a reason for their opinion.
4.support: If she cannot choose, ask her to answer the first three again quickly, so the fourth stands out.
4.challenge: Ask whether she could answer the fourth one in Portuguese, and what she would say.
4.monitoring: Whether she separates a hard question from hard vocabulary.
4.evidence: Which question she found hard, and what she says makes it hard.
4.transition: Move on once she has answered the questions she can and named the hard one.

5.goal: To read one model answer and compare it with what she said to Nina on screen 3.
run: Read the question on the screen with her before she reads: what does Rafa do that she did not do?
Let her read the text once on her own.
Ask the question again and let her answer before you comment.
exact: Before she reads: “Read what Rafa says to Nina. What does he do that you did not do?”
5.expected: He gives reasons (“because I want to study medicine”, “because it shows the bad days too”), he says he is not sure (“Honestly, I am not sure yet”), he has a plan B (“if medicine does not work out…”), he says what he thinks of a series, and he asks Nina a question back (“What about you? What are you watching?”). She may notice the reason and the question back first.
5.support: If she does not find a difference, ask her to find the sentence where he says he is not sure, and then the sentence where he asks Nina something.
5.challenge: Ask which of Rafa's sentences she would not feel comfortable saying, and why.
5.monitoring: Whether she sees the doubt as something useful to say, and whether she notices the opinion about the series.
5.evidence: What she says is missing from her own first try.
5.transition: Move on when she has named at least two differences.

6.goal: To classify six lines from Rafa's answer as a fact, a reason or a doubt.
run: Read the instruction with her: each line does one of three jobs, a doubt, a fact or a reason.
Let her classify the six lines, then press Check.
On each line, ask how she knew. The explanation opens under each line after Check.
At the end, ask what happens to Rafa's answer without the reasons, and without the doubts.
exact: On each line: “Is this something he knows, something that explains, or something he is not sure about?”
At the end: “What happens to his answer if we take out the reasons?”
6.expected: “I am in my last year.” — the fact. “I do biology and chemistry.” — the fact. “Because I want to study medicine.” — the reason. “Honestly, I am not sure yet.” — the doubt. “If medicine does not work out, I would still want something with people in it.” — the doubt. “I really like it, because it shows the bad days too.” — the reason. Without the reasons, Nina has nothing to ask about; without the doubts, he cannot talk about a plan he has not decided.
6.support: On each line, ask: is this something you can check, something that explains, or something he does not know yet?
6.challenge: Ask which of the three kinds she used on screen 3, and which she did not use.
6.monitoring: Whether she can see that the opinion about the series is also a reason.
6.evidence: Which of the three kinds she was already using on screen 3.
6.transition: Move on once the six lines are checked and she has answered the last question.

7.goal: To choose three ways of answering a question she has no prepared answer to.
run: Read the question in the title with her: “What if it does not work out?”
Let her mark the three answers that keep her in the conversation, then press Check.
Point out what the three correct answers have in common: they give a moment to think, and then they say something.
Tell her that “Let me think” is from lesson 20, and that it works here too.
exact: After Check: “What can Nina say after this answer? And after this one?”
7.expected: Keep her in the conversation (correct): “Let me think. I suppose I would do something else with people in it.” · “Honestly? I have never thought about it.” · “I am not sure yet, but I know I want something with people in it.” Close the conversation (not correct): “I do not know.” · “It will work out.” · “Sorry, my English is not good enough for that question.” Students often mark “I do not know.” because it is honest.
7.support: On each answer, ask: what can the other person say after this?
7.challenge: Ask her to give a fourth answer of her own that would also work.
7.monitoring: Whether she sees that the difference is whether there is something left to talk about.
7.evidence: Whether she marked the apology about her English. It can show how she sees her own level.
7.transition: Move on when the three are checked.

8.goal: To write one sentence of each kind about herself, and then say the three without looking.
8.interaction: S writes alone on paper, then says the three to you.
run: Read the instruction with her: three lines, a fact, a reason and a doubt, using the openings on the screen.
Give her a moment to write on paper, in silence.
Then ask her to turn the paper over and say the three lines to you.
If a sentence was better on paper than out loud, say so and let her say it again.
exact: Before she starts: “Take a moment to write three lines about you: a fact, a reason and a doubt. Then turn the paper over and tell me.”
8.expected: Three sentences about her. Possible answers: “I am in my last year and I do… at school.” · “I want to study… / work with…, because what I like is helping people / working with people / being creative.” · “I am not sure yet, but I think I will study… / I think I want to work with people.”
8.support: If she cannot start a sentence, read her one of the possible answers above and ask her to change it so it is true for her.
8.challenge: Ask for a second reason, different from the first.
8.monitoring: The difference between what she writes and what she says.
8.evidence: Whether the spoken version kept the reason and the doubt from the written one.
8.transition: Move on when she has said the three lines without the paper.

9.goal: To give an opinion about a series or movie with a reason, and to ask the other person why, as in lessons 19 and 20.
9.interaction: T–S. You are Nina and give three opinions; she answers each one.
run: Read the instruction with her, and the phrases on the screen.
As Nina, give one opinion at a time, using the prompts below.
After each opinion, she says what she thinks, with a reason, and asks you why. Answer her question briefly.
If she has not seen a title, she can talk about something similar she has watched.
exact: Opinion 1: “I watched Wednesday on the plane. I loved it, because she is new at her school, like me.”
Opinion 2: “I think Inside Out 2 is a bit sad, actually.”
Opinion 3: “Everyone at my old school loved Stranger Things, but I stopped after the first season.”
If she does not ask why: “And you? Do you want to know why I think that?”
9.expected: For each opinion, her opinion with a reason and a question back. Possible answers: “I really like it, because the characters are funny. Why did you like it?” · “Really? I do not think it is sad. I think it is about growing up. Why do you say that?” · “I did not like it, because it is too long. Why did you stop?” · “I have not seen it, but I watched…, and it is really good, because…”
9.support: If she gives only an opinion, ask “Why?” once, and point to the phrase “Really? Why do you say that?” on the screen.
9.challenge: Disagree with her opinion and ask her to give a second reason.
9.monitoring: Whether the reason comes in the same sentence as the opinion, and whether she asks you why without being prompted.
9.evidence: How many of the three opinions she answered with a reason, and how many times she asked why.
9.transition: Move on after the three opinions.

10.goal: To answer four questions she has not seen, in two sentences each.
10.interaction: T–S, quick questions. You choose the questions.
run: Read the instruction with her: two sentences for each answer, the answer and one more thing.
Ask four questions she has not seen. Choose from the list below, or make one from something she said on screen 3.
Let her use the phrases on the screen to get a moment to think.
Do not stop to correct. Note one or two mistakes for screen 12.
exact: Setting it up: “Four questions you have not seen. Two sentences each: the answer, and then one more thing.”

Questions to choose from: “Would you like to study in another country?” · “What would your parents like you to do?” · “Is there a job you would never do?” · “Which subject would you stop studying if you could?” · “Is there a series everyone likes and you do not?” · “What would you do in a gap year?”
10.expected: Two sentences for each question. Possible answers: “Let me think… Yes, I would like to study in the US. I want to see how people live there.” · “Honestly? They want me to study medicine. But I am not sure yet.” · “I would never work in an office all day. I like being with people.” · “Physics! It is really hard for me.” · “That is a good question. Everyone likes…, but I think it is boring, because…” · “I have never thought about it. I suppose I would travel and work.”
10.support: If only one sentence comes, wait, and then ask “And?” once.
10.challenge: Ask one question she cannot have thought about before, for example: “If you could have any job for one day, what would it be?”
10.monitoring: Whether the second sentence comes without the prompt “And?”.
10.evidence: How many of the four answers had two sentences without help.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered four questions.

11.goal: To run the whole conversation, with no support on the screen.
run: Read the instruction and the checklist on the screen with her, then ask her to put her paper away.
Start the conversation as Nina with the first prompt below. Let her talk about herself, then ask Nina's four questions, one at a time, when there is a natural pause.
Ask the question she did not prepare for in the middle of the conversation, not at the end.
Give her space to ask you something. Answer briefly, in character.
Do not correct during the conversation. Note one thing that worked and one sentence to improve for screen 12, and compare what she says with your notes from screen 3.
exact: Starting it: “Hi again! I am Nina. The break is about to end. Tell me about you.”
Nina's questions, one at a time: “So what do you study?” · “And what do you want to do after school? Why that?” · “What are you watching at the moment? Is it any good?”
The question she did not prepare for, in the middle: “And what if it does not work out?”
If she does not ask you anything: “Do you want to ask me something?”
11.expected: A longer conversation than on screen 3, with the points on the checklist: a reason for what she wants to do, one sentence about what she is not sure about, an opinion about a series or movie with a reason, an answer to “What if it does not work out?”, and at least one question to Nina with the correct word order. For example: “I am in my last year. I want to study psychology, because I like helping people. Honestly, I am not sure yet. At the moment I am watching…, and I really like it, because… If it does not work out, I think I would work with people. What about you? What do you want to do?”
11.support: No support on the screen. If she stops twice, ask one of Nina's questions and wait.
11.challenge: Answer one of her questions with something unexpected, for example “I want to be a pilot”, and see whether she asks a follow-up question.
11.monitoring: The number of sentences compared with screen 3, and each point of the checklist separately: reason, doubt, opinion, answer to the unexpected question, question back.
11.evidence: Which checklist points appeared, the number of sentences compared with screen 3, and one sentence to improve.
11.transition: Move on when the conversation comes to a natural end.

12.goal: To give feedback on the conversation and improve one sentence she said.
12.interaction: T–S. You type in the boxes; she says or writes her improved sentence.
run: Type one thing that worked and one point to improve in the first two boxes.
Choose one sentence she said on screen 11 and type it in “First version”, exactly as she said it.
Ask her how she would say it now. She says it out loud, or writes it on paper first.
Type her version in “Clearer version”. Use her words; if something is still wrong, ask a question and let her correct it.
Tell her she will use that sentence in the next conversation.
exact: Asking for the new version: “This is what you said. How would you say it now? Tell me, or write it on paper, and I will put it on the screen.”
12.expected: One sentence improved by her. The improvement is often a reason added (“I want to study psychology.” → “I want to study psychology, because I like helping people.”) or a question with the correct word order (“What you are watching?” → “What are you watching?”).
12.support: If she cannot see what to change, ask what Nina would want to ask next about that sentence.
12.challenge: Ask her to improve it twice: once shorter, and once with more information.
12.monitoring: Whether her idea of a better sentence is about correctness or about saying more. Both are useful; this lesson focuses on saying more.
12.evidence: Her clearer version, in her words.
12.transition: Move on to the next conversation with the clearer version on the screen.

13.goal: To run the conversation once more with the order changed: Nina talks first and does not ask anything, so Gabriela has to start asking.
13.interaction: T–S. You are Nina and talk first; she has to get in.
run: Read the instruction and the checklist with her.
As Nina, talk about yourself and a series you like, using the prompts below. Do not ask her anything.
Leave short pauses so she can get in, but do not invite her.
When she asks, answer and continue the conversation. Let her say her three parts, her opinion and the clearer version of her sentence.
Let her end the conversation.
exact: Nina talking first: “So, I arrived last Monday. My host family is really nice, but the food here is so different! And school starts so early. At home I start at nine.”
Nina's opinion: “Last night I watched Wednesday again. I really like it, because she does not care what people think.”
Nina's plans: “I want to study design, I think. My parents want me to study law.”
If she has not got in after several pauses: “Sorry, I am talking a lot! Do you want to ask me something?”
13.expected: She asks Nina something without being asked first, for example: “Where are you from?” · “What do you miss from home?” · “Why do you like Wednesday?” · “Why design?”. Then she says her fact, reason and doubt, gives her opinion about the series with a reason, uses the clearer version of her sentence, and ends the conversation, for example: “The break is over. Nice to meet you, Nina! See you later.”
13.support: If she has not asked anything after several pauses, use the last prompt above.
13.challenge: Talk continuously and leave only very short pauses.
13.monitoring: Whether she gets in without being invited, and whether she uses the clearer version of her sentence.
13.evidence: Whether she entered the conversation without being invited, and which checklist points she used.
13.transition: Move on to the close when she ends the conversation.

14.goal: To close the lesson and the block, and to compare the first conversation with the last one.
14.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap and tick what was done.
Open “Compare with the start of the lesson” and read it with her. Remind her of what she said on screen 3 and what she said on screens 11 and 13, using your notes.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Ask the last question on the screen: which of the four lessons changed most about the way she talks?
exact: Comparing: “At the start of the lesson you said… At the end you said… What is different?”
The last question: “Which of the four lessons changed most about the way you talk?”
14.expected: Her own reading of the lesson and of the four lessons. For example: “At the end I said more, and I gave reasons.” · “Lesson 20, because now I ask why.” · “Lesson 21, because my questions are better.”
14.support: If she cannot choose a lesson, remind her of one thing from each: opinions with reasons (19), keeping the conversation going (20), questions (21).
14.challenge: Ask what she wants to practice more in the next lessons.
14.monitoring: Whether what she says matches what you observed across the four lessons.
14.evidence: Her answer to the last question, her confidence marks, and your comparison of screens 3 and 11.
14.transition: End here. After the lesson, fill in the Registro pós-aula on this lesson's card, then open the cycle panel (the button after the last lesson card in this tab, which gathers the records of the whole cycle) and check it to confirm how the next block of lessons will be structured.
